units.title: Continued pretraining, mid-training and SFT as distinct interventions, against no-training baselines
outcomes: Choose continued pretraining, mid-training or SFT from the data and behavior gap, rather than from a method name.
Design a comparison against unchanged, prompted and smaller instruction-tuned models with a fixed evaluator and inference budget.
Separate gains from training from gains due to templates, demonstrations or answer parsing.
units.why: A training run is not the baseline. First establish what the frozen model can do, then choose the intervention whose data and objective address the observed failure.

next.note: Turn the chosen intervention into a versioned data and serialization contract.

study.title: Don't Stop Pretraining: domain versus task adaptation
study.locator: Sections 3, Domain-Adaptive Pretraining, and 4, Task-Adaptive Pretraining, including the supervised baseline in Section 3.2
study.depth: Read the data and comparison design, not the full experiment tables. These are masked-LM RoBERTa classification experiments, not causal-decoder SFT results.

focus: Continued pretraining uses unlabeled domain or task text with a language-model objective. SFT uses demonstrations of desired responses. Both change weights; prompting does not.
Mid-training names a stage or recipe, often a targeted mixture and annealing phase. It is not a unique loss, nor a synonym for instruction tuning.

Freeze item IDs, splits, parsing, output-token cap, decoding and template versions before comparing. Different checkpoints may need their own native templates; record that difference rather than forcing a malformed common template.
Match training input tokens and report supervised target tokens separately. Equal optimizer steps do not match exposure when lengths or response masks differ.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write a comparison table for domain-text adaptation versus response-format adaptation. Include unchanged and prompted versions of the same base, an existing smaller instruct model, continued pretraining and SFT. For each row name the data, predicted tokens, changed state, inference budget and held-out target and retention measures. Explain which comparisons isolate training and which compare complete products.
traps: Changing the prompt after training and attributing the full gain to weight updates. Re-evaluate the frozen checkpoint with the new prompt too.
Using a held-out set to tune both the adaptation and its prompt. Keep development and final evaluation separate, with duplicate-group separation.
Treating lower domain language-model loss as proof of better instruction following. Measure the behavior the intervention was meant to change.

selfTest.q: Does training on unlabeled task inputs become SFT because the inputs came from a supervised dataset?
selfTest.a: No. Without the labels or demonstrated responses it is task-adaptive continued pretraining. The objective and target construction, not the dataset's origin, determine the intervention.

selfTest.q: A new chat prompt improves the adapted model. What control is missing?
selfTest.a: The unchanged checkpoint under that same valid prompt and decoding budget. Otherwise prompt elicitation and learning are confounded.

selfTest.q: Why retain a smaller instruct model even though it cannot isolate the adaptation mechanism?
selfTest.a: It tests whether training is worth doing at all under the deployment constraints. It is a product alternative, not a same-initialization causal control.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the frozen, prompted and smaller-model baseline ledger and the prespecified adaptation comparison in `lmlab`.
units.stopWhen: Your comparison table names a measurable behavior gap, a no-training alternative, controlled budgets and a held-out decision rule that could reject training.

fit.verdict: The book supplies the recipe map, DAPT supplies the domain/task distinction, and the mini-project supplies the matched baseline decision.

study.title: Transformers 5.19.0: Chat templates
study.depth: Use only text conversations. Skip tool and multimodal extensions.

focus: A data contract specifies supported roles, message ordering, empty-content policy, truncation, source, rights and split IDs. Role validity is template-dependent; reject unsupported records before training.

Pin PyTorch 2.14.1 and Transformers 5.19.0 for the token fixtures. Use `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` tokenizer revision `c1899de289a04d12100db370d81485cdf75e47ca`, with `enable_thinking=False`; tokenizer checks need no model weights or GPU.

Completed training conversations use `add_generation_prompt=False`. For generation from a final user message, append the checkpoint's assistant header; a prefilled assistant message instead needs continuation semantics.

Direct template tokenization and rendering followed by tokenization with `add_special_tokens=False` should produce the same IDs for the tested record. Save template text and token fixtures with the model artifact.
units.reproduce: Using the pinned Qwen tokenizer, serialize five messages: system `Be brief.`, user `Hi.`, assistant `Hello.`, user `Again.`, assistant `Hello again.`. Compare the `input_ids` from direct template tokenization with rendering then tokenizing using `add_special_tokens=False`. Require exact ID equality. Remove the final assistant message and inspect generation with and without `add_generation_prompt=True`; explain every added control token, including the non-thinking prefix.
traps: Searching decoded text for the word assistant to assign roles. Message content can contain that word or delimiter-like text; ownership must come from structured serialization.
Adding BOS or EOS again after the template already emitted them. Inspect IDs, not just readable text.
Assuming every template supports a system message, strict alternation or assistant masks. Test each capability instead of inferring it from the model family.

selfTest.q: Why is a byte-for-byte rendered string check weaker than a token-ID check?
selfTest.a: Different tokenizer settings can add special tokens or map control strings differently. The model consumes IDs, so rendered equality alone does not prove equal inputs.

selfTest.q: Should a completed training answer get an extra generation header?
selfTest.a: No. It would ask for another assistant turn after the demonstration. The generation header belongs at the inference boundary where a new answer should begin.

selfTest.q: Can instruction and input fields simply be concatenated without a separator?
selfTest.a: Not safely. Their boundary can become ambiguous. Define a deterministic conversion into message content, including the empty-input case, and bind that conversion to the dataset version.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `lmlab` conversation schema, tokenizer/template manifest and train-serve token fixtures, including malformed roles and truncation.
units.stopWhen: Your serializer has exact token fixtures for single-turn, multi-turn, empty-content and truncated records, and a template change fails the train-serve regression test.

fit.verdict: Chapter 4 supplies the conversation contract and the Hugging Face resource family supplies versioned serialization behavior; the mini-project checks the real tokenizer.
